topics.title: Number Systems and Boolean Algebra
topics.syllabus: Number Representations: Binary, integer and floating-point numbers. Combinatorial circuits: Boolean algebra, minimization of functions using Boolean identities and Karnaugh map, logic gates and their static CMOS implementations, arithmetic circuits, code converters, multiplexers, decoders.

cards.title: Identities that actually get used
cards.bodyHtml: Absorption and the second distributive law collapse most expressions in one step. The distributive form x+yz=(x+y)(x+z)x+yz=(x+y)(x+z)x+yz=(x+y)(x+z) has no counterpart in ordinary algebra, which is why it is easy to miss.

cards.title: K-maps and essential prime implicants
cards.bodyHtml: A prime implicant is a group that cannot be enlarged. It is essential when some minterm is covered by it alone — find those minterms first and the rest of the cover follows.
cards.pitfallHtml: A large group is not automatically essential — if every one of its minterms is covered elsewhere, it is redundant.

formulas.noteHtml: check each minterm's alternatives

cards.title: Number representations and complements
cards.bodyHtml: Two's complement is used because addition and subtraction become the same operation and there is only one zero. Its range is asymmetric — one more negative value than positive — and that asymmetry is what most questions turn on.
cards.pitfallHtml: The 1's-complement system has two zeros (000000000000 and 111111111111) and needs an end-around carry. Only 2's complement avoids both, which is why nothing else is used in practice.

cards.title: Adders and arithmetic circuits
cards.bodyHtml: A ripple-carry adder is slow for the same reason it is simple: bit nnn cannot settle until bit n−1n-1n−1 has. Carry look-ahead breaks the chain by computing every carry directly from generate and propagate terms.

cards.title: Decoders, encoders and code converters
cards.bodyHtml: A decoder generates every minterm of its inputs, so a decoder plus an OR gate implements any function directly from its truth table. An encoder does the reverse and needs a priority scheme, because two simultaneous inputs would otherwise produce a meaningless code.

formulas.noteHtml: active-low outputs make it a NAND array, and the OR becomes a NAND

cards.bodyHtml: The maximum clock rate is set by the longest combinational path between two registers, plus the flip-flop's own delays.

cards.title: Shift registers, ring and Johnson counters
cards.bodyHtml: An nnn-bit shift register takes nnn clocks to load or unload serially. The two counters built from one differ only in what is fed back: the plain output gives nnn states, the inverted output gives 2n2n2n.
cards.pitfallHtml: A ring counter uses nnn flip-flops for nnn states where a binary counter needs only ⌈log⁡2n⌉\lceil\log_2n\rceil⌈log2​n⌉. It is chosen for the decoded, glitch-free one-hot output, never for efficiency.

formulas.exprHtml: SISO / SIPO / PISO / PIPO\text{SISO / SIPO / PISO / PIPO}SISO / SIPO / PISO / PIPO
formulas.noteHtml: nnn clocks for whichever side is serial.

cards.title: Finite state machines: Moore and Mealy
cards.bodyHtml: In a Moore machine the output depends on the state alone, so it changes only on a clock edge and lags the input by one cycle. In a Mealy machine the output depends on state and input, so it responds a cycle earlier but can glitch when the input does.
cards.pitfallHtml: Moore outputs are registered and therefore safe to use as control signals; Mealy outputs are combinational and can glitch mid-cycle. A question about a spurious output is almost always about a Mealy machine.

formulas.exprHtml: Moore: y=g(q);Mealy: y=g(q,x)\text{Moore: }y=g(q);\qquad \text{Mealy: }y=g(q,x)Moore: y=g(q);Mealy: y=g(q,x)

formulas.noteHtml: binary encoding; one-hot uses one per state and simpler next-state logic

formulas.exprHtml: statesMealy≤statesMoore\text{states}_{\text{Mealy}}\le\text{states}_{\text{Moore}}statesMealy​≤statesMoore​
formulas.noteHtml: Moore often needs extra states purely to hold an output.

cards.title: SRAM vs DRAM
cards.bodyHtml: SRAM holds its value in a latch, is fast, and needs no refresh; DRAM stores charge on a capacitor, is dense and cheap, and must be refreshed.

formulas.exprHtml: SRAM 6T,DRAM 1T+1C\text{SRAM }6\text{T},\qquad \text{DRAM }1\text{T}+1\text{C}SRAM 6T,DRAM 1T+1C
formulas.noteHtml: SRAM needs no refresh and is used for cache; DRAM does, and is main memory.

cards.title: Sample-and-hold, and ADC architectures
cards.bodyHtml: An ADC needs its input to stop moving while it converts, and a sample-and-hold is what stops it. The requirement is hard: the input must not change by more than half an LSB during the conversion, which for a fast signal is a far tighter constraint than the sampling theorem.
cards.pitfallHtml: Flash is O(2n)O(2^n)O(2n) in hardware and O(1)O(1)O(1) in time; SAR is the reverse. A question giving a conversion time and asking which architecture it is, is testing exactly that trade.

cards.title: Addressing modes, datapath and pipelining
cards.bodyHtml: The datapath does the work and the control unit tells it when; pipelining overlaps the two so a new instruction starts before the last has finished. The speed-up is never quite the number of stages, because the pipeline has to fill and then keeps stalling.
cards.pitfallHtml: Splitting a pipeline into more stages shortens the clock but adds latch overhead and lengthens the branch penalty. Past a point the deeper pipeline is slower, which is why stage counts stopped growing.

formulas.exprHtml: EA=base+displacementEA=\text{base}+\text{displacement}EA=base+displacement
